STEEL COMPANY OF CANADA EMPLOYEES- CONCILIATION BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last I promised a reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) as to whether a request had been received from the united steelworkers union to convene a joint conference of the steel manufacturers and representatives of the steelworkers union to discuss the matter of wage increases. I think the best answer would be for me to refer my hon. friend to Hansard of September 12, 1945, page 111, where my colleague the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) answered a similar question put by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
I feel that I should, however, state that negotiations are going on in respect to em-

Judges Act

ployees of the Steel Company of Canada of Hamilton. At the suggestion of the Minister of Labour for Ontario, Hon. Charles Daley, a conciliation officer was appointed and reported that a conciliation board should be constituted.
The board has been established, the members being His Honour Judge M. A. Millar, Mr. J. S. D. Tory, K.C. and Mr. J. E. McGuire.
I have not as yet received a report from the conciliation board. However, I have every expectancy that a solution will be found.
Of course, the conciliation board will not be dealing with the question of wages. The employees are asking for increases and will, of course, apply through the regional board for Ontario, and, if dissatisfied with the decision, may appeal to the national board.
I am informed the situation is that the application is under consideration by the regional board at Toronto.
I should mention that negotiations are going on in connection with an application for an increase in wages of certain employees of the steel mill at Sydney. In this case a decision of the Nova Scotia regional war labour board has been appealed to the national board and a hearing is scheduled to take place in a few days.
Under the regulations those doing the collective bargaining for the employees in the various steel plants are as far as I am aware conducting their business through the boards established for this purpose in the regular way, and I am very hopeful that a mutually satisfactory settlement of all differences will be reached.
While I am answering the question of the hon. member for Vancouver East on this subject, I deprecate "strike talk". Every once in a while I read in the papers or hear on the radio that someone, and I often wonder who the someone is, is predicting a strike. In my judgment it would be much better if the predictions were all to the effect that a settlement was going to take place. Indeed it might not be out of place, Mr. Speaker, to mention that out of 3,478 cases which have been before the national and regional labour relations boards, strikes have only taken place in eight cases which in my judgment is a very good record, and I compliment both labour and management for this record.

subtopic: JUDGES NOT TO ACT AS COMMISSIONERS OR ARBITRATORS-TO BE BOUND BY DECISION OF COURT OF FINAL APPEAL

speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved for Aave to introduce bill No. 13, to amend the Judges Act.

subtopic: JUDGES NOT TO ACT AS COMMISSIONERS OR ARBITRATORS-TO BE BOUND BY DECISION OF COURT OF FINAL APPEAL
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: JUDGES NOT TO ACT AS COMMISSIONERS OR ARBITRATORS-TO BE BOUND BY DECISION OF COURT OF FINAL APPEAL
speechtext:
The proposed bill amends what is known as the Judges Act, chapter 105 of the revised statutes of 1927. The amendment consists of two sections. Section 1 provides that judges appointed by the parliament of Canada are not to act as commissioners or arbitrators on any commission or inquiry. The frequency of recent years with which judges are drafted for all kinds of such work impairs the efficient administration of justice and sojne-times causes congestion in the law courts, and, as they are largely only fact-finding commissions when appointed, they duplicate the efficient powers and functions of parliament, of the committees thereof, and of the many outside boards of recent innnovation in war work. This causes delays; and they are slowly building up a system of judicial commission government in Canada.
The second section deals with judges to be bound by decisions of the courts of final appeal-the privy council or any other court of final appeal; the decisions of such courts are authoritative. The legal maxim or doctrine known as stare decisis is adopted in this amendment, and this bill will be law for all Canada, notwithstanding the provisions of any law, statute, usage, custom, or doctrine of law to the contrary. Decided cases which lay down a rule of law are authoritative and must be followed. Decisions of the judicial, committee of the privy council, as the court of last resort, will be binding on all Canadian courts.
Motion agreed and bill read the first time.

"dominion"
Mr. A. P. COTE (Matapedia-Matane) moved the second reading of bill No. 8, an act respecting Canada day.
He said: In proposing the second reading of the bill I shall not venture upon any remarks which will give rise to a protracted debate. When Dominion day was established by law as a national holiday our country was, for all practical purposes, and I have reference particularly to the 49th parallel as well as the whole expanse of the ocean, regarded as a possession or as a colony or as a plantation of the British crown, at least according to some constitutional and legal authorities,
Canada Day

among whicli is a unanimous judgment of the Court of King's Bench delivered by Lord Chief Justice Mansfield in 1774.
But since by the statute of Westminster in 1931, which statute constituted a new charter for the nations comprising the six kingdoms, Canada has achieved a new status, from the constitutional point of view the most important event since confederation. And quoting . Dr. Maurice Ollivier in his book entitled "Problems of Canadian Sovereignty":
The statute of Westminster was therefore the confirmation of the Balfour declaration at the imperial conference of 1926 to the effect that the dominions had now become "autonomous communities witiiin the British empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another, in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations."
Therefore the appellation which may have been considered appropriate before 1931 cannot any longer be used to designate properly either our country or the day devoted to its national holiday. Furthermore, "dominion" is surely not an identification which is proper to make Canada known in its true perspective, or in 8ny way at all either to Americans or to other peoples of the world. May I quote here my best authority, our distinguished Prime Minister:
Incidentally, may I say that the time has come to cease speaking of "the dominions" as if they were some peculiar half-fledged type of community, and all alike in their interests and views. Such a usage leads to confusion at best, and to alibis and misrepresentation at worst. South Africa is South Africa, New Zealand is New Zealand, Australia is Australia and Canada is Canada'.
Replacing the word "Dominion" by the word Canada, as far as our national holiday is concerned, will at least provide Canadians travelling outside of our country with * an answer when quizzed about our national holiday-that there is a Canada day and it is on July 1, and on no other day; because for so many strangers Dominion day may as well mean New Zealand day.
The time has come, I firmly believe, our valiant men of the three armed forces having put Canada in the limelight all over the world during the conflict which has just ended, when the name of Canada should be kept in the ears and in the eyes of mankind, and at least of Canadians. Because, for a great many loyal new Canadians and perhaps for a greater number of our older citizens and their posterity, Dominion day means no more than an ordinary bank holiday. Surely it is not too early to try to give the idea to all Canadians that on July 1 they commemorate their

national holiday in a true Canadian way, and that their citizenship is being given a significance on that day. I believe that Canada day bears out that message better than Dominion day.

Bill No. 8 proposes to amend a general act regarding public holidays which has been in force since confederation. In the first meeting at Charlottetown of the fathers of confederation they were unanimous in agreeing that the proposed confederation be called the "Dominion of Canada". From time immemorial we have been a dominion. We are part and parcel of the British empire. There is no reason why this bill should be introduced at this time. If the bill passes, all the history books will have to be changed. Moreover the bill is ultra vires of this parliament, because the original provinces came into confederation on a definite bargain. Speaking at Kingston in 1844, Sir John A. Macdonald said that it has always been the policy of Canada that as a dominion we are part and parcel of the British empire. Long may it continue. Had it not been for that fact we would have had the awful horror of war on our own soil. As I pointed out the other night, not only in Ontario but in Quebec and the maritime provinces we owe it to confederation that that did not happen.
I see no reason for this bill at this session of parliament. There are many bills being proposed with regard to a change in status, autonomy and sovereignty. A large body of public opinion in this country is very much alarmed at what this parliament is doing in that regard. I believe a large body of public opinion in all the provinces is against this bill. We have good history books in Quebec and in all the provinces. Confederation was brought about with the cooperation of the French people of Canada.. Sir John A. Macdonald, Cartier and all the others, Liberals and Conservatives alike, made confederation possible. We have got on very well together. Like Your Honour, I have always believed in confederation and the doctrine of the old Cornish battle cry, "Each for all and all for each". What is good for one province is good for all.
The words "Dominion of Canada" were wisely selected after a great deal of consultation and thought. While we are part and parcel of the British Empire the ties are invisible under our status of autonomy and sovereignty. A million men went from the dominion in the first great war. One hundred and thirty thousand died on the field of battle. We shall always remember France, where several thousand of my own citizens

Canada Day
are buried until the resurrection morning. I plead with hon. members from Quebec to pay-tribute where tribute is due-to Britain for saving our shores from invasion. I see no reason why we should bring up such matters as this at the present time. There are more important economic matters to be decided by this parliament so that a lead can be given to the health, peace and prosperity of all our citizens. We are wasting our time on a lot of secondary matters for political purposes that could very properly be left over until the more important matters affecting the poorer classes of citizens in all the provinces, namely, housing, health matters, fuel, clothing, food, employment, and so on, have been dealt with.
I am prepared to move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross), that the bill be not now read a second time but that it be read this day six months hence.

I wish to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). At the present time I see no reason why we should repeal the Dominion Day Act. We are the Dominion of Canada, and Dominion day signifies something; it signifies the bringing together of all the provinces of Canada in one great country, the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext: The debate is continuing.
The house has before it a bill proposed by the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote). I read the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church).

Is the six months' hoist
debatable?
Yes.

For seventy-five years we have had Dominion day. All our history springs from the joining together of all the provinces of Canada, one by one, and
that is the day which we celebrate. We celebrate the bringing together under Macdonald and Cartier of the two great races of this country. I see no reason why this controversy should be injected into oui national life. Many people will take sides on this matter. All of our children know Dominion day; they have been brought up to know what it means. Our history books show what it means. To me Dominion day means that we have a great nation. I have much pleasure in seconding the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I wikh to congratulate the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote), who introduced this bill. We in Ontario have known the hon.. gentleman for many years as an advocate of real, virile Canadianism and a true friend of Canadian unity. I also appreciate the views of hon. members from the city of Toronto, and give them credit for sincerity in their attitude toward this question. However, I do take issue with them when they state that this is not an important matter.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to rise in support of this bill, because I sincerely believe that by its adoption we can make a real contribution to Canadian national life. To-day we look out on a troubled world, a world bleeding and suffering after six long years of war. Here in our own country we have problems so perplexing and of such magnitude that sometimes I confess to a feeling of discouragement. I submit that in dealing with our national problems and in facing up to the problems of the world we must get down to a consideration of fundamentals. One great need in Canada to-day is for a patriotic siprit of determination to win the peace, comparable to the splendid spirit of patriotic determination shown by the people of Canada in the winning of the -war. During the war years the Canadian people met every challenge with which they were faced during the most trying period in Canadian history. It did not matter whether the challenge was in connection with men for our armed services, whether is was in connection with money for victory loans, for the Red Cross, for munitions and supply, for food or for whatever cause it may have been; the challenge was successfully met, no matter what the sacrifice. That was the spirit in which we made our splendid contribution toward the winning of the war, and I submit that is the sort of spirit we need to win the peace.
During the long, trying years of conflict we spoke freely and hopefully of the new era which was to come after the war. The men in our fighting forces on the far-flung battle lines throughout the world were encouraged and buoyed up by the belief that they were
Canada Day

fighting for a new world, a new era which they, their comrades and their loved ones at home would enjoy. They looked forward to that new day which would come when the forces of evil, as represented by our enemies, would be destroyed. Those enemies 'have been destroyed, and now we must face up to the fact that the post-war era of which we spoke so much is here. Many of the boys who fought our battles have returned; more are returning, and there are still more to come. But as we welcome them back to our communities; as we talk with them about their reconversion problems and the difficulties they face in reestablishing themselves in civilian life, we cannot help being impressed by the sincerity of their concern for our national future. And I think if we are completely honest we must admit that as we talk with them they tell us the truth when they say that so far they see more signs of the old era than of the new.
It is true that our government has made a valiant reconversion effort in the face of most difficult world conditions. It is true that this effort has been successful to such an extent that with pride and truth we can declare that we in Canada are better off than people anywhere else in the world. But this is not enough. We are still far short of the ideal of a better life and that new era which we pictured during the years of war. In attaining that ideal we must not be hampered by an unwillingness on the part of our people to make sacrifices for peace comparable to the sacrifices they were willing to make for war. I regret to have to confess that I can see signs of a tapering off of our national willingness to make sacrifices to overcome the problems of peace. It is indeed sad, if it be true, that we in Canada need the threat of falling bombs to inspire our best national endeavour; but unfortunately there is evidence that this is so. In plain language, what we need is a substitute for falling bombs to inspire the best efforts of our people.
I do not suggest that by the simple adoption of this measure designating our national holiday as Canada day we can perform a national miracle, but in all sincerity I do submit that the taking of this step at this time can be made the basis of a crusade for a revitalized national spirit which can contribute a great deal to the future well-being of Canada. Thanks to the sacrifice of our people, the name "Canada" to-day stands high throughout the world. In this, the greatest conflict of all ages, our fighting men went into battle bearing on their armour the name "Canada". The bill the house is now asked to approve simply provides that 
our national holiday shall bear that same glorious name, "Canada". It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, most fitting, following the measure passed by this house decreeing that Canada should have its own distinctive national flag, and following the bill so ably and eloquently introduced the other day by the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) providing a new status of Canadian citizenship, that this house should follow through now and adopt this bill designating our national holiday as Canada day.

Mr. Speaker, it did my heart good to hear a good Presbyterian from the city of Toronto support this bill. When the word "Dominion" came into existence I do not think it had the approval of one of the greatest Canadians to have adorned the history of this country; I refer to Sir John A. Macdonald. I quote from the Encyclopedia of Canada:
Dominion, the term adopted in 1867 to describe the status of Canada in the British empire, and now used to describe also the status of Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Newfoundland. The story is told that the adoption of the term was due to a suggestion of Sir Leonard Tilley (q.v.) When the delegates from Canada, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia, were discussing in London, in December, 1866. the details of the British North America Act, some difference of opinion arose as to the proper term to be used to describe the new federation. Sir John Macdonald, the leading Canadian delegate, was in favour of styling it "the Kingdom of Canada"; but Lord Derby, the British foreign minister, was afraid that the word "Kingdom" would wound the tender susceptibilities of the people of the great republic to the south of Canada. The Canadians, on the other hand, were firm in rejecting the term "colony." The night of this debate, Sir Leonard Tilley, who was in the habit of reading a chapter of the bible before retiring to rest, stumbled on the verse in the seventy-second Psalm which runs, "He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth." The next morning he suggested that the new federation should be called "the Dominion of Canada."
To me the name Canada has music in it. To me it represents the greatest country on earth. If there are any here who have made Canada their home, but who think that old England, Scotland or Ireland are superior to Canada, then I wonder why they left there. Ireland to me was a tender spot on this earth, but I left it and came to Canada because I thought it gave the greatest possible opportunity to the young man, greater than any other country on earth. We had lots of opportunity.
To me the name of Canada is emblazoned across the world, and stands out as the country that is going to lead in a great many things. We cannot be too careful in changes we make, but some of us are not as conser-

Canada Day
vative as we were forty years ago. I believe we should pass this legislation, and have our children sing of Canada-not only of the Dominion of Canada. Therefore I support the bill.
There is the British North America Act, first.

Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope that this does not develop into an issue which will divide the house along party lines. I should like to make some practical observations, and would state first that all the good things which have been said about Canada have come to pass at a time when we have paid tribute and reverence to the name "Dominion of Canada." So it is difficult for me to see where there would be any advantage in a change of this kind.
I listened to the hon. member for York North (Mr. Smith) say that he has noticed a tapering off in our enthusiasm. I have not been able to see that among my people. I know North York pretty well too, because there I cut my political teeth, and I am pretty well satisfied that the people in North York are not lacking in their enthusiasm.
I think the hon. member who introduced the bill did not consider the matter fully. I challenge him or any other member in the house to name any country in the world which calls its national day by its title. I have not heard of any other country-and of course I may be wrong. But at the moment there come to my mind names of such countries as the United States, Mexico, Russia and France. I believe the title we already have, that of the Dominion of Canada, is all right.
Replying to the hon. member who introduced the bill, may I say I am not so much concerned about what strangers may think of us. After all, we have our own lives to live. They will come to know us from our contributions, as they have in the past, and from the contributions we shall make in the future. I am inclined therefore to support the view offered by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) in his amendment, when he points out that there are items far more important to be discussed and determined than the mere changing of a name, and especially a name which has been used and enjoyed since we became the Dominion of Canada.
Dominion day is well known to Canadians generally, and to those who have any regard for us. I hope there will be others who will feel as I do-not in any partisan sense, but in the belief that we are well designated now, and that our national day should remain Dominion day.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended speaking on this bill, but I do so because I' have a sentimental reason for saying a few words. My good friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), mentioned that it was Sir Leonard Tilley who first recommended that our country be called the Dominion of Canada. Sir Leonard Tilley came from my native province of New Brunswick, and was born in the village of Gagetown, which happened to be my own birthplace, and my own home.
Two great men from the same town.

We love Canada:	Canada is our country.
But we do not want to break our link with the past, or to dim the traditions of other years. And I say we are fast doing it.
One other hon. member said that we have perplexing problems. True, we have. And I would ask that hon. member how many jobs it will give returned soldiers if the name of, Dominion day is changed to Canada day. How many houses is it going to build for the thousands of men who are coming back to this country to change the name of Dominion day to Canada day? It is absolute nonsense to suggest that it will do anything of the kind.

Mr. Speaker, I claim the same right as the hon. member who spoke a moment ago and who suggested that our great perplexing problems could be solved by changing the name of Dominion day to Canada day. I shall say no more. Canada is steeped in the traditions of the past, and if we are to sever all the links with our past history, Canada will never be the great nation we all hope she will become.

Mr. Speaker, this bill seems to be engendering a good deal of heat. I cannot understand why it should, or why there should apparently be conflict between one side and the other.
What I have been asking myself is whether the bill is in order. When confederation was established, four provinces entered into it; the British North America Act records their names and states that they became united into one dominion forming the Dominion of Canada. Those provinces were Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario. Would it not be necessary to have the consent, first, of the province of Ontario and of these other provinces before we could pass a bill such as this? I know you would not easily get the consent of Ontario; it may come some time, but I do not think Ontario would jump hastily and accept this change holus-bolus without careful consideration. I do not know that the province of Quebec would. The province of Quebec played an important part in forming c<*nfederation; in fact, confederation could not have been formed if Quebec had not consented to it. Has the province of Nova Scotia consented to this bill? Has the province of New Brunswick consented to it? I am just wondering, Mr. Speaker, if the bill is in order and whether it would have any effect if we did pass it without the consent of the provinces having first been obtained. I should

think that one of the ministers, perhaps the Secretary of State, under whose department this matter comes, would be able to tell us whether the provinces have been consulted and whether they approve this change in the name of the country of which they agreed to form a part. If they have not been consulted, perhaps the hon. member should withdraw his bill.
I want to sa.y a word about the hon. member. I compliment him on his ability. I have been greatly pleased since this present parliament assembled to note how many splendid bright and capable young men we have in it representing the province of Quebec. I know of no other parliament since I came here in 1930 in which there have been so many able young men from the province of Quebec, and that is all to the good. They are doing well for their province, and will continue to do well. And so I do not want my hon. friend to think that in opposing his bill I am in any way finding fault with his proposal, but I still ask myself how can we pass this bill if the provinces have not first been consulted. If the bill moved be given its second and third reading to-day, the legislature of Ontario is now in sesion, and would it not be reasonable to expect that some member of the Ontario legislature would ask the govern-of this province if they had consented to changing the name from the Dominion of Canada to Canada-because the British North America Act, Mr. Speaker, all the way through, refers to the Dominion of Canada.
When Manitoba came into confederation it was as a province of the Dominion of Canada, and the same is true of British Columbia. Those two provinces, and later Saskatchewan and Alberta, but particularly Manitoba and British Columbia, which entered confederation quite early, all entered the Dominion of Canada. Have they been consulted? Have their legislatures approved the changing of the name of the country of which they became a part?
This does not change the name of the country.

Yes. We are going to change the name "Dominion day" to "Canada day". The Dominion of Canada is the name that I have known every since my childhood. When the first of July was celebrated in the small town in which I was raised it was always celebrated as Dominion day, and so Dominion day has become a part of me. I would have to change my whole fifty odd years-I am not going to say how many, Mr. Speaker, but

will say fifty or fifty odd years, of my life's thinking to celebrate Canada day instead of Dominion Day.
I yield to no one in my love for Canada. I am of the fourth generation here. My hon. friend the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) is perhaps of the seventh or eighth or tenth generation. I cannot go back that far, but I am of the fourth generation, and I love Canada.
I really cannot understand why my hon. friend the member for Matapedia-Matane brought in this bill, and further I cannot understand how it comes before this house if the Secretary of State or whoever draws up these bills did not first consult the provinces which originally entered confederation, to find out whether they wished to make this change from Dominion day to Canada day. It is a matter of importance, and therefore, Mr. Speaker, although I have a very warm regard for the capable young man who introduced this bill, I must say that I cannot vote for it.

SINNOTT (Springfield)':	Mr. Speaker, I have a veiy friendly feeling for the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who has always been most cooperative in this house, but coming from Manitoba as I do I must say I feel that we are a part of Canada. We are no longer in the days of 1867, when confederation was formed. I think we should be progressive. A year or so ago the Conservative party in this country progressed by adding the word "Progressive" to its name. I think we should progress, too, by making this change from Dominion day to Canada day and letting the outside world know that we have something. There is no harm in letting the outside world know that there is such a place as Canada, and there is no harm in letting the western part of the dominion know that we are a part of Canada. Coming from the western part of this dominion I shall give whole-hearted support to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would not have risen to speak on this bill had not the hon. member for York North (Mr. Smith) said that it was a great bill, and the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) said that there was no harm in letting the world know that there is such a place as Canada. If the idea of a great bill is to change the name Dominion day to Canada day, and if by that change we are going to let the whole world know that there is such a place as Canada, one must think very little of Canada; for ever since confederation we have been known as the Dominion of Canada. Dominion day to me represents the accomplishments of a great people, in a great country 63260-361
under great leadership, who formed this dominion in the year 1867, and the word "unity" has always been the keynote in the celebration of Dominion day. Dominion day has been taught, to me at least, to represent the day on which the people of Canada celebrate the union which made Canada, the accomplishment of the great men who achieved its unity. For an hon. member to stand up and say it is a great bill which does away with the word "dominion", a word1 which appears in every one of our statutes, marking the significance of Canada as a dominion-because the word "dominion" means unity, cooperation, amity and friendship on the part of us all-makes me wonder what is in the minds of those who want to change the name. What is wrong with the word "dominion"? Certainly "Canada" is a great name. Certainly Canadians are proud of Canada. But surely before we become proud of Canada we must be proud of the union which made Canada, of the idea of a dominion in and of Canada.
I do not like to hear hon. members say that those who do not wish to abolish the word "dominion" are not progressive. I do not like to hear them say that those who do not wish to supersede "Dominion day" by "Canada day" think any less of their country than others do. I do not believe there is anybody in the country who does not feel that "Canada" and "dominion" are two different thoughts, both to be held with reverence, with esteem, with love, and with pride. But I do not think we should be "little" about it, either. When I see the hon. member for York North (Mr. Smith), that old historic riding, that community which has done so much for Canadian history, which has been so loyal to the Canadian union and to the Dominion of Canada, get up and suggest, at least by inference, that the word "dominion" implies something inferior, something sinister, something undesirable, something unprogressive, I believe other hon. members should rise with pride and insist that we stick to the word "dominion", show our pride in the word, show our reverence for Dominion day as a day symbolizing unity, confederation and friendship. If you want a Canada day, surely you can pick another day. If you want to tell the world that Canada is a great nation, do so, but without changing the thought which commemorates reverence, friendship, and the historic things which Dominion day represents.
I heartily support the amendment and would oppose changing the word "dominion", because it means much to the people of Canada; it has a significance which we would lose if we changed .the name.

Mr. Speaker, for the information of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MaeNicol) I would refer him to the British North America Act, section 3:
It shall be lawful for the Queen ,by and with the advice of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, to declare by proclamation that, on and after a day therein appointed, not being more than six months after the passing of this act, the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick shall form and be one dominion under the name of Canada; and on and after that day those three provinces shall form and be one dominion under that name accordingly.
Also section 5:
Canada shall be divided into four provinces, named Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick.
Those four provinces were Canada. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher) asked, what is wrong with the word "dominion"? When we refer to the dominion we refer to a member of the British commonwealth of nations, but not particularly to one country; the idea implies a plural; it includes such dominions as Australia and South Africa as well as Canada. But if we. have the name "Canada" it will refer to our own country, our beloved country, and will not be a name which applies to other countries. I support the motion.

Before the question is put I desire to say just a few words, and in the course of my remarks it is my desire to ask permission to move the adjournment of the debate, but not at this precise moment. That motion is one that I am sure, when I do put it, I shall not need to write out and present to you, Mr. Speaker, fhe difficulty which occurred in the case of another lawyer's handwriting when he wrote "second" and it looked like "third." Probably if I were to write it you would have as much difficulty in reading my writing as you do in reading that of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). But it will not be necessary.
A few remarks have been made to which I will advert for a moment. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MaeNicol) remarked that this debate seemed to be engendering a great deal of heat. I agree. And he said it did not seem to be necessary that that should be so; and with this, too, I agree. For my part I believe I have had and have now as much pride in this country as has any person in the house. I do not suppose I am preeminent in that respect; I think all of us look upon ourselves first, last and all the time as Canadians. I have not found it difficult to develop that pride in my country

because it was called the "Dominion" of Canada. I do not think there is quite as much importance in this name as some have said. Nevertheless I agree with the bill; I agree that it would be better to make the change, as the bill sets forth. I think the word "Canada" is a more appropriate one for our national holiday than the word "Dominion."
Some people have spoken as if the Vord "dominion" suggested that some person else had dominion over us. It never had that meaning for me. I have never felt that "Dominion of Canada" carried the idea of some people remote from here exercising dominance over us. I do not know whether it is because of the story of how the word came to be chosen that I have been free from that idea. My recollection of the story as it was told to me is that one of the founders of confederation, in considering what would be a suitable name for our country, either was praying or was thinking of God, and the words came into his mind. "He shall have dominion from sea to sea"; and thereupon he took that as an inspiration and brought the word into the conclave, and so "Dominion" came to be adopted. As I recollect it, some such sfory as that is the basis of the choice of the word "Dominion". I do not know whether that is the particular kind of dominion which some would like to escape by discarding the word. I do not fancy that it is.
The truth of the matter is that we should not confuse the word "dominion" with dominance, and there is no dominance of any person or any power to be considered as a concept in connection with that word. At the same time, I do not think that some of the expressions that have been used this afternoon are apt. The member for Broadview spoke of our having been a dominion from time immemorial. That, it is self-evident, is not so. We have not been a dominion from time immemorial, nor have we been a dominion during most of the existence of organized society on this northern half of the continent. We have been a dominion because that was the name decided upon in 1867. That is all there is to it. It looked like a suitable name at the time, and it served well enough over the years. We have developed much pride in our country in the use of that name, but it does not carry the idea of autonomy which is the fact respecting Canada at the present time. It would be better, I submit, that we should try to keep our terms in accord with the facts of our situation. We are an autonomous country, all our partners in the British empire agree with that, and it would be well in the use of all expressions to convey the

idea which does express the truth of the matter. For that reason I submit that we would be wise to change the name. There is no thought, nor need there be any thought, that in making the change there is any attack upon the British connections or any disrespect for the crown, or any flying in the face of tradition or anything of that sort. It simply appears to me that we would be nearer to the truth if we used the expression "Canada" in naming the day which is our birthday.
I revert to what I said at the beginning about there being some heat in the debate. I submit that we would probably be well advised to wait a few days and come back to the question rather than settle it now, and for that reason I move the adjournment of the debate.

I doubt whether this bill is within the power of this parliament because it is contrary to the British North America Act, and the terms and principles on which the four provinces came into confederation, and if the word "Dominion" is changed, the change must have the approval of the provinces. There is no power to change it. The history books prove that, and we have the confederation debates and records. It was unanimous at confederation to name the country the Dominion of Canada.
We had a scene this afternoon unparalleled since I have been a member of this house. The members of the cabinet were divided. If the government followed the practice in the old country it would resign, because a government in the old country resigned at one time when it was defeated on a private member's bill or a motion at one stage of it.
Where is this going to land us? Where does Canada stand when one considers the motions we have had on the order paper in the past few months and the debates that have gone on? What was said regarding the future of this dominion by members of the government from the province of Quebec who are absent from the house to-day? Either we are a dominion or we are not. If not, we-are outside the British empire. We were a dominion at confederation when the four provinces came together. There was none of this bickering during the two wars. I referred to that earlier in the afternoon, and I shall not repeat what I said. I do not think the people of any of the provinces believe in altering the terms and conditions which were agreed to by the four original provinces at confederation. Those terms cannot be changed without the consent of the legislatures of the various provinces. This is a political bill, first, last and always. Either we are in the British empire or we are not. We do not wish to be like Eire. We are a dominion within the four corners of the British North America Act. If we do not wish to be a dominion we should say so. I am surprised at my hon. friends of the C.C.F. and the attitude they took on this bill this afternoon. There is a large body of public opinion which is alarmed and surprised that this parliament finds time to devote to all these matters which are frivolous and secondary. I voiced their opinion this afternoon. We have not time to attend to the primary matters which are facing this country to-day. There are some people without houses,
employment, coal, food and clothing. These matters should be primary and not secondary. That relates to all the provinces.
I have always been one of those who believe in the principles of confederation, of equality and each for all and all for each. I do not know who drafted this bill. Whoever drafted it has forgotten the act of confederation which constituted this country and the intention of the four provinces. The change cannot be made without a vote of the provinces. Hon. members can talk all they like about this, but we are still part and parcel of the British empire. We ought to be thankful for that, especially those who come from the eastern provinces. Britain, save for the dominions, stood alone for two and a half years. The people of Quebec have always been loyal and faithful to the British crown. They showed it in the revolutionary war of 1783 and have always shown it. I have a great deal of respect for Quebec and for France, where so many of the old soldiers of the city from which I come lie buried. They were quite ready to fight for that great country. France will always be a glorious nation. Mr. Churchill said that and I have said it in this house on many occasions. It is the hope of the world that France should be restored as a great nation which she has always been in the past. At a time when economic and social conditions are so critical in this country I object to debates of this kind, more especially when our people are suffering from the after effects of the war. It is inconceivable that we should waste time on bills of this description.
I think the afternoon was well spent, however, because the people in the mother country are wondering where Canada stands at the present time. Is she willing to help the mother country, where so many thousands of churches and public buildings, destroyed during the war, need to be restored? Are we to sit here as a parliament and not observe the handwriting on the wall? Are we not going to listen to those who are clamouring for us to deal with the great economic problems, to start production, to bring about adequate reconversion of industry, instead of wasting our time on things like this?

I should like to say a word to account for the manner in which I have voted up to the present. I quite agree with the previous speaker that this procedure is unconstitutional. In spite of the fact that we have taken all afternoon to debate this matter, I do not believe the proposed change will be made. I think when we come to deal with the proper authorities the holiday will still be observed as Dominion

Canada Day
day. Those who feel we have to change the name in order to advertise Canada to the world certainly cannot know what has been going on during the past few years. I can assure them that anyone who has been in the midst of what has been going on since the fall of 1939 will readily realize that the young men and women of our three armed services have certainly advertised this dominion in no uncertain terms in all parts of the world.
I repeat that in my opinion this procedure is quite unconstitutional; therefore I do not believe this parliament should take time to debate a matter of this kind when, if we are really concerned about changing the name, We might easily adopt the proper procedure.
Which is what?
First of all, I think the British North America Act probably will have to be changed.
Why?

I am not a legal man, and I am not going into that question; but, as an hon. member said a few moments ago, at least we want time to consult our constituents. I am satisfied that if the people of this nation take the performance this afternoon seriously their reaction will come as a rude shock to many people here.
Oh, oh.

I am just as entitled to my opinion as any other member of this house. It may be that I am not able to judge properly the feelings of my constituents back home, but I am prepared to endeavour to do so, and am prepared to stand by their decision with no regrets whatever. I am one of those who believe this has been quite a political gesture this afternoon. I do not believe the name will be changed, but I wanted to make these remarks in order to explain the stand I have taken to-day.

I am very much in accord with what has been said by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. For some reason or another an attempt has been made to rush this bill through, and I think the people of this country as a whole should be given an opportunity to decide, by their reaction, whether or not it should become law. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary West, that the Chairman do now leave the chair and that the committee do now rise.
Motion negatived: yeas, 31; nays, 75.
[Mr. J. A. Ross.l
I am certain that this bill is of a great deal of importance in the life of Canada, perhaps more so than some hon. members realize.
That is right.

This bill is important
because it shows a trend which I think must be faced by the Canadian people and which I am sure will be faced. Taken by itself it may not mean a great deal whether our national holiday is known as Dominion day or Canada day, but we must take into consideration the circumstances under which this bill comes before the house. Here we have it brought in with many signs of a desire for haste, a great urge to put it through.
No; you cannot say that.

You can make your own speech. There were clear evidences this afternoon that the cabinet did not know what to do about the matter, that the cabinet were divided. No opportunity has been given to Canadians, certainly none to the people of my province of British Columbia, to consider this bill, and no request for this change has come from that province. I doubt whether any request for a change has come from any province in Canada. It must be taken, too, with the different statements that have been made in this house. To those of us who sit here it is only too obvious that an attempt is being made at this time to take actions which, while I know those sponsoring them believe they are in the best interests of Canada, at the same time may have a. serious effect on Canada if we look at the broader picture. We have just gone through a terrible war. At one stage of that war civilization was only saved by the British empire, and-
"Only"?
What about the Canadians?

What about the
Americans?
-because the empire stood together for a whole year, when nobody else was fighting the Germans and Italians but the British people of the world, and gallant little Greece.
What about France?

We have won this war, and it Was a close shave; everyone in the house

Canada Day
admits that. Since that time we have been faced with attempts only too obvious to break up the British empire from without-
No, no.

I said, "from without." It is just as plain as can be that there is an attempt by certain other nations to squeeze the empire out. If the empire should be squeezed out, if it should be broken up, then indeed that would be a tragic day for Canada as well as for other nations of the empire.
This is no time to be doing things that will weaken the empire, because the future of Canada depends upon the empire's being strong. I doubt very much whether my good friends who are cheering and shouting, and who are so keen to have this bill rushed through have ever had in mind the possibility that action of this type of necessity weakens the empire.
No, no.
Oh, you may not agree with me, but-
We don't.

-surely in a British
parliament a member who has been duly elected has a right to be heard, and not to be heckled.
We have been elected too.
We are listening.
You are not listening with any measure of comfort. You are interrupting, which you have no right to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I remind all hon. members that an hon. member who is speaking must not be interrupted or questioned without his consent. May I also remind hon. members that when speaking they must address the Chair.

For these reasons I suggest that we be very careful before we rush into a thing of this type.
I have listened to a great deal of talk in this and in the last session about colonially-minded Canadians. The challenge has been hurled across this floor on different occasions that those of us who believe in a strong empire are colonially-minded, that we are colonials. Let me suggest this to the house, that the shoe might be on the other foot, and that it might 'be those Canadians who refuse to recognize the value of the empire to Canada who are colonially-minded, and who have not got over the old colonial days which passed away many years ago.
It does not do for members who talk in that way to get the idea that they are the only Canadians in the world. Let them remember that there are many of the rest of us who are just as good Canadians as they are, and who come from a long line of Canadian settlers. Let them remember that we are just as good Canadians as any others in the country, just as much interested in the welfare of Canada, just as much determined that no other nation shall come first in our minds, whether that nation happens to be within the empire or outside it.
We are just as much in earnest about this question as any other people in Canada. I think it should be recognized by all Canadians, no matter of what origin, that those who sit in the House of Commons, no matter what side they may be on or what their beliefs may be, are all good Canadians, and are all working for the benefit of Canada.
Therefore I suggest that some hon. members be just a little careful in throwing out those charges, when they say, "Oh, you are only colonials; you are not good Canadians; you are Englishmen first"

or Australian-"and Canadians second." Those charges are not correct.
Since I have been a member in the house there has been much talk about unity. It seems the suggestion is always made that the English-speaking people in the country must be very careful or they will upset unity, that they will bring about disunity in Canada. Charges are always coming in that direction. Well, if this sort of thing is carried on much further, the shoe will be on the other foot. English-speaking people in Canada are going to think they are being attacked.
Who made those charges?

My hon. friend can read Hansard. I say they are going to think they are being attacked. If that should come about-and, fortunately, it has not yet-but if it should come about, and if it should develop that one great group is set up against the other great group, then there never will be unity in Canada.
Imagination!

There never will be unity in Canada, I say, if that should happen, and our troubles will become greater and greater; we shall never build a nation in this country if that should come to pass.
For that reason I make my appeal to all hon. members in the house-and I have friends in all the parties, friends of many years
Canada Day

standing. I would appeal to them not to keep pressing through measures of this type which can only make trouble. Yes, they can only make trouble, and especially when the attempt is made, as it was made to-day, to rush this thing through.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
No.
Why didn't you vote against it, then?

An attempt is being made to rush this thing through. I wish the people I represent could have sat in the galleries here to-day to see just what has happened, because it is impossible to convey it in words. That sort of thing is bad for Canada. It will make all kinds of trouble in Canada, and I would-
You are making it.

-appeal to hon. members not to rush to put a measure of this type through the house.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, during the dinner recess I have had an opportunity of considering this bill further and I feel that there are some observations still to be made.
Throughout our whole history our thoughts and sentiments have been associated' with Dominion day, and not with anything of any semblance to Canada day. I made a challenge to this house this afternoon when the Speaker was in the chair to name any country which calls its national day after the name of the country. In the United States, for instance, their national day is called "Independence day," and the same holds good with respect to every other country which celebrates a national day. Dominion day has been associated with the birth of this nation ever since 1867, to designate that we were a dominion within the great commonwealth of British nations.
The word "dominion" means something to a Britisher. After all, you cannot have your cake and eat it. Either we are a part of a great empire or we are just an individual nation. I prefer to associate myself, as I believe the majority of the members of this

house do who think seriously on this matter, with the broadest application of the word "dominion."
A few days ago I had a commander in the navy visit me and he made this remark. I mention this in relation to what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver South. This navy commander said, "If I lived a thousand years and' spoke or lectured every night I could not begin to tell of the great contribution made by the British people in those trying daj% of the war when Britain stood alone."
During my limited experience in public life, confined largely to municipal affairs where government had its beginning, I have never imputed improper motives to my fellow man. I have nothing but the highest regard for the hon. member who introduced this bill and for those who are supporting it, because I believe that they are imbued with a sense of loyalty to Canada and that they, too, have in their breasts deep affection for and a sense of loyalty to that one great nation in the world which stood between us and tyranny in the darkest days of the war. I do not believe that they would want to see any weakening of the ties which bind the empire together as a great world power, although I regret to say that there is a tendency in this critical hour to weaken those ties. But in unity there is strength, and the greatest strength we enjoy to-day is our association with the British commonwealth of nations. This great empire stands for something which Britishers and freedom-loving people throughout the world cherish. I could not find words to express adequately what the British empire has stood for and what it has meant in human relations throughout the world, but I am thinking of one thing in particular at the moment, and that is freedom. Unfortunately, never having been denied our freedom, we sometimes do not value our freedom highly enough; but if we were to travel throughout central Europe and talk with the thousands there who were deprived of their freedom and became a subjugated race, it would readily be appreciated what a great heritage of freedom is ours to enjoy. When the Prime Minister of this country, quite properly in my opinion, took a definite and determined stand with respect to espionage in this country, I wonder just what our position might have been had we been a small individual nation unprotected by our position in the empire. What answer might we have received from a great power at that time if we had been just a small nation standing alone? But because we knew that we enjoyed the protection and the support of one of the

Canada Day
greatest empires the world has ever known we were able to make our voice heard, and *even though criticism was heaped upon the Prime Minister of this country, Canadians generally I think gloried in the courageous stand he took. By that I am not implying any approval of the methods adopted. I am not a legal man and I am not going to argue legal points, but I say that in the main public opinion admired the Prime Minister for championing the nation's cause because the security of individual Canadians was at stake.
The other night the Minister of Mines and Resources, in reply to the hon. member for Davenport, who had a bill before the house to introduce a Jack Miner day, said in effect that it was a matter which involved the provinces because it touched upon education. He thought there should be a reference made to the provinces before the house should give its assent to that bill.

Mr. Chairman, you handicap me in what I intended to say, because, if that was important then, this is far more important now. When the provinces of Canada joined in confederation there was designated a day termed "Dominion day", "Dominion of Canada day", or any other like expression you wish to apply to it. Surely the provinces have now the right to determine whether this house should write upon the statute books of this country the substitution for "Dominion day" of the term "Canada day".

Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? It is not correct to say that in 1867 Dominion day was designated as such. In 1867 the reference was to "Canada", but in 1879 a resolution was introduced in the upper house urging that July 1 be made "Dominion day". That resolution was subsequently dealt with in this house on motion of a private member!
I thank the hon. gentleman for giving me the chance to make the observation that in 1867, July 1 was not designated as "Dominion day", but simply referred to in sections 3 and 5 of the British North America Act as "Canada".

I accept my hon. friend's explanation. I believe that it lends strength to my argument, for it indicates that in 1867 they were not in a position to determine a suitable day or a suitable designation for a day; but after some years had elapsed, they in their wisdom-and after all they were the makers of Canada and of confederation-determined that it should be called "Dominion day". I am glad to have the hon. member's explanation, but as far as I am concerned any sentiments I have with respect to Canada's national day are directly associated with Dominion day. I consider that the mover of this resolution would have had a great deal more support in this house if he had sought to have the day termed "Confederation day" rather than "Canada day". If we adopt and pass this bill we shall be the only country in the world which uses our national name to designate our national day. I leave that thought with the committee. The world is in a formative, unstable state. What we may do now in this direction may tend to weaken the strength we need in these trying times. I do not want to be misunderstood. I believe my Canadian friends of French descent from Quebec will give me credit for speaking from my heart, just as I believe they have spoken from theirs. Canada as part of the empire has played a great part; I cannot agree in in any way with the hon. member for York * North that an act of this kind would make it any greater. Canada's history is written in the contribution she has made to world affairs. Her sacrifices have been made under the terms of an act and are commemorated by a day which we are now seeking to change. I hope someone will see fit to amend this proposal so as to change "Canada day" to "Confederation day", as being something which better describes the purpose we have in view. I do not want to be bigoted in my views. I believe we have in this house a sense of common loyalty; we have all sworn allegiance to the same crown; we believe in British institutions, British laws and British justice. We are therefore not very far apart. I suggest that the title proposed in a wrong one and will be misunderstood, and this thought I leave with the Chairman and members of the committee.

I did not intend to participate in this debate, but I think it is my privilege to try to correct an impression which was made by the remarks of some hon. mem-
Canada Day

bers this afternoon. I do not for a moment question their sincerity. I do not for a moment doubt their good faith in their argument. But it seems to me that these remarks follow the same policy which has been adopted by members of the Progressive Conservative party, who always claim, whenever we try to enact legislation which has for its purpose to develop or better emancipate Canada, that we are trying to destroy our British connection. They have always followed that policy. Whenever any change was suggested or contemplated in the relations of Canada to Great Britain, those who are interested in having things remain as they are insist that we are trying to put an end to confederation. This has been said about practically every constitutional change since the conquest of Canada. In 1927, when the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, then leader of the Conservative opposition, opposed the appointment of a Canadian minister to Washington, he did so on this very ground. His actual words were:
ft the last great adventure in our relation to the British empire. It is but the determining of separation; it is but the end of our connection with the British empire.
And, Mr. Chairman, when Mr. Bennett jame into office in 1931 he appointed his own brother-in-law, Mr. Herridge, as minister at Washington. Mr. Herridge served his term, and I do not believe it is the opinion of my hon. friends that any material change was made in our relations with Great Britain.
It was also suggested this afternoon that before the adoption of the British North America Act there was an agreement by which this country was to be called the "Dominion [DOT] of Canada . I do not believe that this assertion is true. In order to substantiate my opinion I wish to refer first to a book entitled "The Constitution of Canada", by Kennedy, on page 314 of which the author states:	'
When the conference resumed after the holidays Lord Monck, the governor general, and .Lord Carnarvon, the colonial secretary, attended its meetings accompanied by Sir Frederic Rogers afterwards Lord Blachford, the permanent under-secretary. Attempts were at once begun to draft a bill. With the final resolutione before them, at least six drafts were drawn up. The seventh and last printed in imperial form was dated for revision February 9. 1867, and was the outcome of consultation between the imperial representatives and the members of the conference. Perhaps the most interesting fact about these drafts is that at first the name of the new federation was left to the decision of the queen. Later it appeared as "the kingdom of Canada," and in the final draft as "one dominion under the name of Canada." Macdonald was the ruling genius" with power in "management and adroitness." There can be little doubt with his strong bias in favour of a legislative union that he desired to f6rm an auxiliary kingdom out of the colonies, and he deplored in later [Mr. Pinard.l
life the lack of insight which rejected the title. He fought hard for its retention, but it was withdrawn at the instance of Lord Stanley, the minister for foreign affairs, who feared that "it would wound the sensibilities of the Yankees." It was appropriate that the name of Canada should be chosen in preference to the fantastic titles suggested by the press, but history does not relate from what source or for what reasons the word "dominion" was added.
May I now quote from one who, together with Sir George Etienne Cartier, may well be considered the founder of confederation. I refer to none other than Sir John A. Macdonald. I wish to quote from a book entitled "Correspondence of Sir John Macdonald," by Sir Joseph Pope. At page 450 there appears the following:
The declaration of all the B.N.A. provinces that they desired as one dominion to remain a portion of the empire, showed what wise government and generous treatment would do, and should have been marked as an epoch in the history of England. This would probably have been the case, had Lord Carnarvon, who, as colonial minister, had sat at the cradle of the new dominion, remained in office. His ill-omened resignation was followed by the appointment of the late Duke of Buckingham, who had as his adviser the then governor general, Lord Monck-both good men certainly, but quite unable, from the constitution of their minds, to rise to the occasion. The union was treated by them much as if the B.N.A. Act were a private bill uniting two or three English parishes. Had .a different course been pursued-for instance had united Canada been declared to be an auxiliary kingdom, as it was in the Canadian draft of the bill, I feel sure (almost) that the Australian colonies would, ere this, have been applying to be placed in the same rank as the kingdom of Canada.
I should like to quote the postscript:
On reading the above over I see that it will convey the impression that the change of title from kingdom to dominion was caused by the Duke of Buckingham. This is not so. It was made at the instance of Lord Derby, then foreign minister, who feared the first name would wound the sensibilities of the Yankees. I mentioned this incident in our history to Lord Beaconsfield at Hughenden in 1879, who said. "I was not aware of the circumstance, but it is so like Derby-a very good fellow, but who lives in a region of perpetual funk."
Who wrote that? .

That was written by Sir John A. Macdonald and addressed to Lord Knuts-ford on July 18, 1889, and it is reported in Sir Joseph Pope's "Correspondence of Sir John Macdonald."	>
I submit, therefore, that it is not right, in fact it is definitely wrong, to assume that the title "Dominion of Canada" came into being as a matter of agreement. That is not the fact. The name "Dominion of Canada" came into existence as the circumstances which I have stated indicate.

Canada Day
There is another aspect to this matter, and I mention this in answer to the argument which was advanced this afternoon and which has been repeated to-night by the same hon. member, namely, that no other nation has adopted as its holiday a day bearing its name.
I do not think that is the purpose of the bill. The purpose of the bill is to attempt to clarify an ambiguity which has existed for a considerable time. When Dominion day is celebrated and the first of July is taken as the day of celebration it is apt to lead any one to think that the first of July might as well be the holiday of any other dominion forming a part of the British commonwealth of nations. When in the future any other country may become a dominion and form .part as an associate of the British family, this argument will again, I suggest, be advanced and we shall again be caught with the same ambiguity. It will then be considered that "dominion day" may be the holiday of any other dominion forming a part of the British commonwealth of nations.
Personally, it was with pride that I voted in favour of the second reading of the bill. It is with joy that I wish this country of mine, Canada, to have as its national day a day which, like the fourth of July in the United States or the fourteenth of July in France, will be known the world over as the holiday of our own country.
It is with confidence in the future of Canada that everyone in this country, all of us who in the near future will, I hope, become Canadian citizens by virtue of the new citizenship bill which has been introduced, should approve this all-Canadian and most progressive legislation.

I did not intend to take part in this debate because I have been here only one session before and, in my short experience of bills introduced by private members, any such measure has been talked out. I did not know at the time that the government would rally so vigorously and enthusiastically to the support of this particular bill and therefore I did not take part in the debate prior to the time the vote was taken. Since the dinner recess I have made some investigation to find out when Dominion day was originally instituted, and I find that it was on May 15, 1879. On that date an act of parliament was passed which first introduced Dominion day. I should like to quote from the preamble:
Whereas it was on the first day of July that the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick became one dominion under the name of Canada; and
Whereas Rupert's land and the northwestern territory and the province of British Columbia became part of the dominion in the month of July, and Prince Edward Island became part of the dominion on the first day of July; and
Whereas it is expedient that such important events should be commemorated:
Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows.
Then appears what we find in the present bill. I find that in the old debates there was not one dissenting voice. The matter was brought forward in the house, and Mr. David Mills, a resident of western Ontario, made this remark:
Dominion day was, he believed, universally kept as a holiday, at least, it was in western Canada, but it was not kept under the authority of any act of parliament.
I suggest that this act, which has been in force for sixty-seven years and under which Canada has made great advances, should not be changed and that no change should be made in the name of this particular holiday.

I find it very difficult
indeed to understand why so much heat is generated over a proposal of this description. Surely we have come to the day when, setting aside all prejudices, we ought to be prepared to recognize this country as Canada. I look back over the years and I find that in 1867 the proclamation which proclaimed the union of the various provinces of this dominion into one great confederation referred to our country as Canada. I find that when Sir Robert Borden, the erstwhile leader of my friends to the right, signed the treaty of Versailles in 1919, he did not sign it in the name of the . Dominion of Canada but in the name of Canada. The various agreements that we have made over the last number of years have been made in the name of Canada. Surely the men and women who went overseas in this war did not carry on their arms any insignia of colonialism; they carried on their arms the name of Canada. For the life of me I cannot understand why there are hon. gentlemen who rise in this house and still desire to cling to the name "Dominion", when dominion has a connotation altogether different from that which is the connotation of the word "Canada" to-day. Canada is a nation. Canada has grown to nationhood in the last seventy or eighty years. Canada- has earned a place in the comity of nations and deserves to be recognized as such. It seems strange to me that nearly every other country in the world, including the United Kingdom, recognizes this country as a nation as Canada. Yet we have people in our own country who refuse to recognize it. I cannot understand it.
Canada Day

I came to this country as an immigrant from Great Britain thirty-six years ago. No one can say that I have no love for the country which gave me birth; but this is the country in which I have found my life, in which my children were bom. I want to see Canada assume that spirit and place ,of nationhood which is rightly hers. I cannot understand my hon. friends who continually cling to the outmoded connotations of colonialism.
A few moments ago a quotation was given from the writings of Sir John A. Macdonald. May I requote it? Sir John A. Macdonald was writing to Lord Knutsford on July 18, 1889. He went on to explain why it was the name of the kingdom of Canada was not accepted, as my hon. friend has placed on the record already. In the postscript which I should like to place on the record anew we find these words:
On reading the above over I see that it will convey the impression that the change of title from "kingdom" to "dominion" was caused by the Duke of Buckingham. This is not so. It was made at the instance of Lord Derby, then foreign minister, who feared the first name would wound the sensibilities of the Yankees.
My hon. friends Who are objecting to the use of the name "Canada" are apparently still carrying on the tradition that we must not wound the sensibilities of the Yankees. As far as I am concerned, I do not mind wounding the sensibilities of the Yankees or of anybody as long as this country may assume its proper place among the nations of the world. I continue with the quotation:

As far as I and those who are associated with me in this party are concerned, while we want to retain the very closest friendship with the people of the United Kingdom and the people of the British commonwealth of nations, we nevertheless want to see to it that this country of ours, Canada, shall be known throughout the world as Canada and not as the Dominion of Canada with a colonial connotation. Therefore I support this bill; I want to se it go through.

been trying to build a nation. Persons from all over the civilized world have come to this country from time to time. Our boys who fought overseas were proud to bear the name of Canada.
